newsitem.title: HUNGARY: GE's Hungary bank says sell-off row harms business.
newsitem.headline: GE's Hungary bank says sell-off row harms business.

text.p: General Electric's Hungarian banking unit Budapest Bank on Wednesday appealed to Hungary's politicians to end their criticism of the way the bank was privatised in 1995, saying the negative press reports were harming its business.

"The controversy is having some adverse impact on our employees and customers," Budapest Bank Chairman George Tappert told a news conference, adding that the recurrent criticism was likely to have been triggered by political motives.

General Electric's GE Capital Services unit bought a 27.4 percent stake in Budapest Bank in 1995 December. The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development acquired a 32.4 percent stake in the same time but GE received controlling rights in the bank.
The privatisation has drawn sharp criticism from opposition politicians who said the bank was sold too cheaply at 12 billion forints ($87 billion).
The sale followed a government capital injection of the same size earlier in 1995.
A parliamentary investigative committee last year unveiled irregularities in the capital injection but no action was taken.

The controversy was re-ignited when it was disclosed late last year that in the privatisation contract the government undertook to repurchase assets worth 8.2 billion forints from Budapest Bank at the bank's discretion.
Last week, a leaked draft State Audit Office report said that the state had lost 16 billion forints as a result of the privatisation of Budapest Bank.
Tappert said that in 1995 the sale was favourable for both GE and the government which had tried unsuccessfully to sell the bank for two years.
He added the bank was successful despite the negative press reports, and GE remained committed to make it the "most productive and customer-responsive" bank in Hungary.

As a result of an austerity programme introduced in 1995, Hungary's economic performance improved substantially and this helped the state to privatise banks in 1996 and 1997 at increasing prices, the government said earlier.

The state privatisation agency APV announced on Wednesday that it would sell a stake in Kereskedelmi Bank (K&H) to the consortium of Belgium's Kredietbank and Ireland's Irish Life for a price of a record 567.3 percent of the face value.
